item.title: Crude oil settles at $80.17. Trades at its lowest level since August 26.
item.description:
WTI crude oil fell nearly 4% Monday, trading near $80.20 a barrel around settlement after reaching an intraday low of $79.95. The selloff extends a slide that had already pushed crude to three straight weekly declines. So what gave sellers the upper hand today?

  • Libya’s Sharara pipeline reopened. Libya’s National Oil Corporation told Reuters that crude had begun flowing into storage tanks at Zawiya. The restart adds to supply availability at a time when traders are already watching for a surplus.
  • The market is looking ahead to more supply in 2027. The October rebound in Middle Eastern exports left more crude on tankers, and JPMorgan expects additional production from the Middle East outside Iran and from the Americas to contribute to a surplus next year. The bank sees oil futures in the high $70s in the first half of 2027.
  • A stronger dollar added a headwind. The dollar rallied alongside the Nvidia-led rebound in stocks. That makes dollar-priced crude more expensive for buyers using other currencies and added pressure to a market already selling off on supply news.

The telling part of today’s move is that crude fell even after reports of fresh attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Traders put more weight on the barrels coming back into the market and the prospect of more supply next year. The next policy event is the November 29 OPEC+ meeting, when producers are due to discuss 2027 output.

For traders, $80 is the immediate barometer. Trade above is more bullish. Trade below is more bearish. 

On the downside, if the price moves lower $79.62, $76.53 and $74.24 are all targets. Move below that level and the low from July at $67.24 will be eyed. That low was near the closing level on February 27 - the day before the start of the US/Iran War. The market will be interested in that level.  

For your guide, the current average price for a gallon of gas in the US is $3.63. It was at $4.29 a month ago.  The price on February 28, the day the war started? The price as at $2.98 per gallon.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Jensen Huang may be back but the China hawks probably haven't given up
item.description:
Charles Gasparino is out with an interesting report. He argues that the Nvidia saga isn't over and for reasons that could rattle the equity bulls.

He writes: 

The weekend at the White House was pure bedlam, people with direct knowledge of the matter tell me, with many major tech CEOs and many on Wall Street intensely lobbying the White House and Trump to push harder for Jensen Huang to return to prevent and AI market meltdown, my sources say. Huang meanwhile continued his own push to return and needed that national security pass from the administration to do so and got one. But thee people add this story is far from over because of everything we known about Nvidia’s biz and stuff that is coming out including its accounting issues and how it dealt w China. 

The drama is no surprise but this is a concern:

  • Accounting issues
  • How it dealt with China

Now it's not clear that "stuff that is coming out" means news we already know about or conjecture but it's a reminder that there are powerful forces that don't like how Nvidia has behaved and don't want to see Huang succeed. Now maybe it's China hawks in a power play and they've now had their wings clipped or maybe the people fighting against open source AI really want to take Huang down.

So now we just have to wait for the next round of leaks. No one likes to hear about accounting leaks and the vendor finance is a real problem.

Shares are up 30% today but they've flatlined from the open. When people hear about accounting issues, they're inclined to take some off the table.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The Nvidia reversal creates a fresh scramble for dollars
item.description:
I wrote recently about the rise of the chip-dollar as a driving factor in foreign exchange.

Today, we are seeing it again. There is a major risk-on trade underway but the euro and pound are both notably lower against the dollar. In fact,the euro is trading at the lowest levels since April 2025.

Now a big part of that is that Europe has been ineffective at growing its economy or fostering any kind of competitive technology sector. Where ever the profts flow from AI, it's not likely to be to Europe.

In addition, there are increasing social and fiscal problems that repeatedly flare up with many in markets thinking that will soon manifest as regime change in the French government, and perhaps elsewhere. In short, Europe doesn't really have an identity for investors.

But the AI story is a different lever for the trade as the dollar is strong essentially across the board. The view is increasingly two-fold:

1) The US will win in AI and if you want to invest in AI, it will be USD

2) The US is tilting towards unrestrained power, and will use AI to exploit that

Essentially -- as today's actions on Nvidia show -- the US has been captured thoroughly, and at every level, by forces that are determined to win and determined to drive stock markets higher. Now you can talk about the inevitable blowback and consequences of that -- both foreign and domestic -- but in the interim, it's likely to work.

When you listen to White House chief of staff Steven Miller, the messages is clear. The US will dominate whatever it wants and will exploit its power for the benefit of the United States. The rules-based order of the world is over and that basically means there are no rules. This is self-evident if you've been paying attention but the question is whether or not it's permanent.

My view, increasingly, is that it is. Republicans may lose the White Hosue in the next election but the seduction of unrestrained power, constantly re-writing the rules and exploiting it all for short-term financial gain is impossible to resist. In a world where the rules are arbitrary, you want to hold the currency and assets of the people making the rules.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold rebounds 3.2% despite a stronger dollar and higher yields.
item.description:
Gold is up 3.2% today, trading near $3,654 after falling more than 9% last week and hitting its lowest level since September 2025. The rebound stands out with both the US dollar and Treasury yields moving higher. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no interest. So why is gold higher anyway?

The stock market rebound may be helping indirectly. As AI and chip stocks tumbled last week, some investors sold gold to raise cash and meet margin calls. With Nvidia leading a sharp rebound in equities today, some of that selling pressure may be easing. Gold was already recovering before the US stock market opened, suggesting dip buyers were stepping in early. I’d characterize the move as a relief rally after last week’s liquidation, with the improvement in risk sentiment helping it along.

The 50% retracement is now the barometer.

Technically, last week’s selloff took gold down to the upper edge of a swing area near $3,500. The price reached $3,502 on Friday before bouncing. Today’s low came in higher at $3,533.80, and the rebound has since taken gold back above $3,610.01, the 50% retracement of the move up from the 2022 low. The rally extended to $3,689.47 before pulling back.

For traders, $3,610.01 now defines the close risk. Stay above it and the buyers keep the short-term bias, with today’s high at $3,689.47 the first upside hurdle. Move back below it and the break loses traction, putting today’s low at $3,533.80 back in focus, followed by the $3,500 area that held on Friday.

In the video above, I take a more detailed look at where buyers stepped in, why the 50% retracement matters, and the levels that will tell us whether this rebound has more room to run.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: U.S. Treasury sells $69 billion the two-year notes at a high yield of 4.700%
item.description:
The US treasury sold $69 billion of 2-year notes:

  • WI level at the time of the auction: 4.703%
  • High yield: 4.700% vs 4.708% at the prior auction
  • Stop-through: -0.3 basis points vs the average stop-through of -0.1 basis points
  • Bid to cover: 2.65X vs the average of 2.63X
  • Directs: 38.1% vs the average of 31.98%
  • Indirects: 51.5% vs the average of 56.51%
  • Dealers: 10.4% vs the average of 11.50%

Auction grade: B−

The auction stopped through the WI by 0.3 basis points, reversing the 0.3-basis-point tail at the prior auction. Bid to cover was just above average. The standout was direct demand, with bidders taking just over 6 percentage points more than usual. That more than made up for the shortfall in indirect participation and left dealers with a smaller share than average. The stop-through and lighter dealer takedown give the auction a B−.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The EURUSD is moving below a retracement target and to the lowest level since April 2025
item.description:
EURUSD has extended to a new low for the day, moving back below the swing area between 1.09041 and 1.09499. In the process, the price also broke below the 61.8% retracement of the move up from the January 2025 low to the January 2026 high. That retracement comes in at 1.09048, just seven-tenths of a pip above the bottom of the swing area.

That puts two technical levels in nearly the same spot. The 1.09041 to 1.09048 area is now the first barometer for buyers and sellers. Stay below it, and the bearish bias remains intact. If the price moves back above that pocket and holds, the immediate downside pressure eases and buyers get room to work back through the swing area. They would still need to get and stay above 1.09499 to take more control.

What’s next on the downside?

The session low at 1.08880 is the first level sellers need to get through to extend the move. Below that, there’s little obvious support on the daily chart until the late-March 2025 low near 1.07337. That makes 1.07337 the next major downside target if sellers can keep the pressure on.

Education. How to use a broken level to define risk

When a swing level and a retracement sit this close together, watch how the price behaves around both on a retest. Here, a bounce that stalls near 1.09041 to 1.09048 would show that sellers are defending former support as resistance. A move back above both levels that holds would raise the risk of a failed break and give sellers a reason to reassess.

The two levels serve different purposes. The 1.09041 to 1.09048 area gives sellers a nearby level to lean against. The top of the swing area at 1.09499 is the bigger test for buyers. Knowing which level you’re leaning against lets you define your risk before the next move develops.

In the video above, I take a more detailed look at the break, the levels buyers need to reclaim, and where sellers can define their risk from here. Watch the video to see how those levels line up on the chart.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: A look inside Anthropic shows there is no ceiling on AI
item.description:
The market had a meltdown over AI fears this month and there is a real discussion to have about the economics of the AI spend.

At the same time, the real story of AI is the technology itself. It's the most important technology in a generation or it might not but another technological revolution at all. It may be the technology that accelerates every technological revolution that follows or came before. While AI stocks were falling apart in markets, there were two critical revelations that show us where we're going.

1. Anthropic gives all access to METR

On November 5, METR released a report from the inside of Anthropic. It didn't get the attention it deserved because it was released at the same time as the US midterms, in the midst of a 5% Nasdaq fall and it was seen as pre-IPO hype.

This was a mistake. METR is the best-placed independent evaluator there is and Anthropic gave them unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process for a period from August 12 to October 29. They were basically let inside the company and shown its secrets. They were allowed to publish their conclusions, while Anthropic restricted details (and METR agreed).

Here is what they concluded:

  1. Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025
  2. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D (this is close to recursive self-improvement)
  3. And critically "We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months."

In short, there is no wall. AI is going to continue to progress at an even-faster pace in the next year.

Critically, METR said it was confident that the observed acceleration was not simply the result of faster growth in training compute, which has been the bearish argument.

2. The Riemann hypothesis

Not many people in markets understand the gravity of AI solving a 167-year-old math problem but Anthropic did it late last week and it's now been verified. This is basically the holy grail of math problems and it is likely to unlock entirely new ways of looking at math. Brian Conrey, a leading Riemann specialist, told AFP: "It's really the biggest thing I think that's ever happened in mathematics."

But beyond math itself, this solution shows that AI is far more capable than we realize of breaking down new barriers. It's a validation of CEO Dario Amodei's promise to cure diseases.

If AI can help solve a mathematical problem that has defeated the world's greatest minds for 167 years, what other seemingly intractable problems are suddenly within reach? The implications for scientific discovery, from materials science to medicine, are difficult to overstate.

If a problem this difficult can be solved by AI, it can fix much of what ails complex systems today. Moreover, if METR is right, then we are going to see more problems solved by AI at an increasingly fast pace.

The significance of these two developments together is hard to overstate. METR has shown that AI is already accelerating the development of AI itself, while the Riemann hypothesis breakthrough illustrates the kinds of problems that increasingly capable models can tackle.

Most-recently, there has been talk about a leap in robotics training from AI. That's the kind of thing that underscores the value AI is creating.

Now, will it go to memory chip makers? Or graphics chip makers? Power producers? Hackers?

That's an entirely different discussion and a difficult one. I continue to think the HALO trade is the safest bet on AI. Rather than trying to pick the winners in a rapidly evolving AI arms race in an ever-changing sea of volatile sentiment, I'd rather own businesses with durable assets, economic moats and limited vulnerability to AI disruption, but plenty of opportunities to benefit from the productivity gains. These are companies that can easily be disrupted by AI but they can benefit from it.

The greatest winners from AI may not be the companies selling intelligence, but the companies that suddenly find intelligence becoming almost free. But starting valuations always matter so that's why the job of traders will always be timing. Given the recent rout, it's worth taking a look at everything today.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD trades to new 2025 highs and stretches toward the next targets
item.description:
USDCAD is pushing to its highest level since April 2025 as broad US dollar buying and higher Treasury yields give the pair another lift. The 2-year yield is up 9.36 basis points, while the 10-year yield is up 3.4 basis points. Markets are now pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a Fed rate hike in December. At the end of last week, there was still about a 6% chance the Fed would leave policy unchanged.

US stocks are also rebounding sharply, with the S&P 500 up 4.84%, the Nasdaq Composite up 6.64%, and the Nasdaq 100 up 6.84%. The strength in equities is taking some of the immediate focus off last week’s selloff and putting it back on inflation. The jump in the 2-year yield shows where the biggest adjustment is taking place, and that repricing at the front end is helping support the dollar.

November buyers reverse the October decline

Technically, USDCAD has been trending higher in November after spending October moving lower. The pair bottomed at 1.39278 on November 4 and extended to 1.43740 today. That’s a gain of 446.2 pips, or 3.20%, in roughly three weeks of trading.

The broader move higher has come in fits and starts. Since the low around the turn from January to February, there have been several sizable swings in both directions. The rallies, however, have produced higher highs, and the pullbacks have found buyers at higher lows. Last week, buyers cleared 1.42928, the 61.8% retracement of the decline from the February 2025 high to that early-2026 low. Today’s push to a new high for the year extends that sequence.

Where is the stretch point?

On the daily chart, the next target is the 1.4401–1.4414 swing area, where rallies stalled in the second half of March and again in April 2025. Today’s high came within 27 pips of the lower edge. After a rally of more than 440 pips, that area gives buyers a place to take some profit and gives sellers a level to lean against, with risk defined above 1.4415.

For buyers, the test is whether the price can get above the entire area and stay there. A sustained break would open the door for another leg higher. A rejection would put the focus on how much of the latest rally buyers are willing to defend.

What would give sellers more control?

On the downside, the rising 200-hour moving average at 1.42947 sits just above the 61.8% retracement at 1.42928. The two levels are less than 2 pips apart, making them a single area to watch on a pullback. USDCAD hasn’t traded below its 200-hour moving average since November 5. A move below both levels would break that run and give sellers more control.

As long as that support holds, the bias remains with the buyers. The next question is whether they can turn 1.4401–1.4414 from resistance into support.

Education. How to define risk after a trend move

After a 446-pip rally, the daily and hourly charts answer different questions. The daily swing area at 1.4401–1.4414 shows where prior rallies stalled and where sellers may lean again. For sellers leaning against that area, a sustained move above 1.4415 would undermine the trade. If buyers break through and hold the area on a retest, the old ceiling can become a floor.

The hourly chart helps judge whether a pullback is starting to change the trend. The rising 200-hour moving average at 1.42947 and the 61.8% retracement at 1.42928 are less than two pips apart. That makes them one support zone. A dip below the moving average can still find buyers at the retracement. A move below both, followed by a failed attempt to get back above them, would give sellers stronger evidence that they’re taking back some control.

In the video above, I take a more detailed look at the daily and hourly charts, where buyers and sellers can define their risk, and what to watch if USDCAD breaks above the swing area or starts to give back part of its November rally.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The Nvidia news has the broader indices moving sharply higher. How has the moves impacted the technicals?
item.description:
Nvidia shares are trading sharply higher following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and board member. The rally has taken the price back toward $165, putting it inside a key swing area between $164.07 and $168.80. The 50% midpoint of the trading range since the April 2025 low also comes in near $165, adding to the area’s technical importance.

The $164.07 to $168.80 area served as a floor from July 2025 into the spring of 2026. When that floor gave way in November, sellers took control and pushed the price down to $124.50 on Friday. Today’s snapback has brought Nvidia right back to that old floor, where sellers now have a level to lean against.

For buyers to take back more control, they need to get and stay above $168.80. A sustained break would open the door to the next upside target at $183.49, the broken 38.2% retracement, followed by a swing level near $189.80.

For now, $168.80 is the barometer. The news brought buyers back in force. If sellers cap the rally in this area and push the price back below $164.07, the move still fits the definition of a correction into resistance.

The S&P 500 is up about 330 points, or 4.77%, at 7,240. The rally extended to a high of 7,260.17, just above the upper end of a swing area between 7,237 and 7,260 that dates back to May through June 12. The index has since slipped back into that range, putting the focus on whether buyers can get back above 7,260 and stay there.

If buyers can clear that first hurdle, the next upside target is another swing area between 7,300 and 7,321. A break above 7,321 would put the moving average at 7,350.13 in focus. Each of those levels gives sellers a place to lean against. If buyers can break through and hold above them on pullbacks, they would take back more control.

For now, 7,260 is the topside barometer, and 7,237 is the level to watch on the downside. Holding above 7,237 keeps buyers in position for another run at the high. A move back below it would give sellers some room and leave the rally looking like a correction into resistance.

The Nasdaq Composite is up about 1,554 points, or 6.85%, at 24,173. The rally reached an intraday high of 24,269.75, briefly taking the index back above 24,206.50. That level is the 50% midpoint of the move up from the late-March low to the October high. The index has since slipped back below the midpoint, making it the first level buyers need to reclaim.

The midpoint sits near the lower end of a swing area that extends to 24,425.34. That area served as a floor from April until it broke earlier this month. On the way back up, the old floor gives sellers an area to lean against. Today’s high got the index back into that zone, with the upper end still ahead.

For buyers, the first step is to get back above 24,206.50 and hold it. A sustained move above 24,425.34 would clear the entire swing area and give buyers more control. As long as the upper end of that area caps the rally, the move still fits the definition of a correction into resistance.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P Global US services November flash PMI 54.7 vs 55.7 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 57.9
  • Manufacturing 54.5 vs 54.9 expected
  • Prior was 54.9
  • Composite PMI 54.6 vs 55.9 prior
  • Employment rose
  • New orders positive but growth here cooled for a second consecutive month, down to its weakest since July.
  • "Slower growth in part reflected constrained capacity, causing a further build-up of backlogged work"
  • Business output expectations for the year ahead revived from October’s five-month low but remained below September’s recent peak

This is a solid number but there is some downward momentum in this survey.

Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence:

“Although output growth slowed in November, recent readings have been impressively strong, and the PMI surveys still point to GDP rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter. Growth also remained encouragingly broad-based across both manufacturing and services, with both sectors also still taking on additional staff in numbers that are indicative of a further strong payroll gain during November.
“A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November. Supply disruptions, widely linked to global shipping delays, also appear to have become more widespread, adding to firms’ concerns about being able to fulfil orders and likely to add further to underlying price pressures in the coming months.
“The survey also provides insight into business confidence after the midterm elections, and it’s encouraging to see confidence revive from the low seen ahead of theelections in October. But business growth expectations clearly remain subdued by historical standards, with political uncertainty and inflation firmly front and centerof business minds as they look to navigate the year ahead.”

I think one of the reasons that it's tough to see a bear market beyond AI is that there are so many signs that the rest of the economy is solid. Now that can change with rate hikes and the stock market falling but there's a decent starting point here and many boxes ticked that point to a positive outcome. Last week, all the numbers from retail companies reporting earnings were fine (at worst).

For background, the S&P Global's flash US Purchasing Managers' Indexes for manufacturing and services are released at 9:45 am ET, typically about a week before the end of the month. Based on roughly 85% of the month's survey responses, they're among the first indicators of US business conditions for the current month. Final readings follow in the first few business days of the next month and usually differ only slightly from the flash.

The PMIs are diffusion indexes drawn from monthly surveys of senior purchasing executives at private-sector companies. Readings above 50 point to expansion from the previous month and readings below 50 to contraction. The manufacturing PMI is a weighted composite of new orders, output, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of purchases. The services PMI headline is the business activity index, based on a single question about the volume of activity compared with the prior month. A composite output index combines manufacturing output and services activity into one gauge of private-sector growth.

The details often matter more than the headlines. Input prices and prices charged are closely watched as early signals of inflation, showing how much cost pressure firms are facing and how much they're passing on to customers. New orders, backlogs, employment and business expectations give an early read on demand and hiring, and the report's commentary frequently highlights the impact of tariffs, supply chains and policy uncertainty.

The S&P Global PMIs usually carry less weight with markets than the ISM surveys, which have longer track records and a larger following, and the two don't always agree. Their edge is timing and global comparability. Flash PMIs for the eurozone, UK, Japan, Australia and India are released the same day, letting traders compare US momentum with other major economies.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: What next for Nvidia technically?
item.description:
Nvidia shares are soaring after the company reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately. The stock is trading near $165, up roughly 33% from Friday’s low of $124.50. That puts the price right at the 50% midpoint of the trading range dating back to the April 2025 low. It also brings Nvidia back into a swing area between $164.07 and $168.80 that traders have leaned against before.

That swing area was a floor from July 14, 2025, through March 30, 2026. When the price broke below it with momentum on November 13, sellers took control and eventually pushed the stock down to $124.50 on Friday. Today’s rally has brought the price right back to the area where that breakdown started. The old floor is now the ceiling, and $168.80 is the level buyers need to get and stay above.

What do the buyers need to do now?

A move above $168.80 that can hold would give buyers more confidence and open the door to the broken 38.2% retracement at $183.49. Get above that level, and the next upside target comes in at the swing level near $189.80.

On the downside, $164.07 is the first level I’d watch. If the price stalls in the swing area and moves back below its lower edge, sellers who leaned against the old floor would have a nearby level to define their risk. With the stock already up roughly a third from Friday’s low, how it trades around this zone will tell us more about whether buyers can sustain the rebound.

The rally spills over into the broader market

The buying has extended well beyond Nvidia. Nasdaq futures rose more than 7% in premarket trading (up 1752 points), before hitting a circuit breaker and halting. S&P 500 futures are up about 330 points, while Dow futures are up about 1,300 points.

The gap higher puts buyers in control early. For Nvidia, the first test after the cash market opens is whether buyers can clear $168.80 and defend it on a pullback. If they can, the same area that capped the rebound could become a floor again.

Nvidia’s rally spills over to other chip stocks

item.title: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as President and CEO, effective immediately
item.description:
How do we even explain what happened with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang?

He was just reinstated as the CEO and President of Nvidia. Shares of Nvidia are up 26% premarket and the board said it was confident there was no national security risk.

To me, it's clear that China hawks in Washington orchestrated his downfall, possibly without the consent of the President. A series of planted leaks to cooperative journalists were an onslaught that pushed him out.

The motivation was clear: He wasn't doing enough to keep Nvidia chips out of the hands of China. Beyond the financial value of selling more chips, he openly argued that selling chips to China was a better strategy than trying to restrict them. He sharply pushed back against the premise of conceding the Chinese AI chip market, famously stating, "You're not talking to somebody who woke up a loser."

He argued that computing ecosystems are deeply sticky rather than easily swappable commodities, rejecting the mindset that ceding global market share is inevitable.

Washington showed how far they would go to destroy someone who didn't fall in line. In addition to destroying his marriage and reputation, they went as far as to invent a 'Chinese spy" honeypot narrative that quickly unwound.

In any case, the ouster worked. Or at least it did for a time.

The problem is that timing is everything. The China hawks waited until after the midterms, which tells me that it was likely the State Department and Marco Rubio behind it (as rumored) because they didn't want to cause market turmoil ahead of the vote. 

What they didn't count on was that questions about AI economics were hitting at the same time; and inflation was tilting the Fed more hawkish. By ousting Huange at the same moment, they compounded the market's angst and it turned it into a rout. 

As usual, narrative follows price and it has become "the market has gone down because Huang got pushed out". 

Or at least that's the narrative that got to the White House.

If there's one consistent thing about Donald Trump as President it's that he ultimately measures himself against the stock market. He lost his nerve around Liberation Day when stocks went down and will never do anything that causes real pain. He is also someone who likes a quick fix.

So, "the market went down because Huang got fired" is easily solved by "bring Huang back" in the mind of the President. So that's what we got and now we're getting the mother of all pre-market rallies in NVDA.

That optimism has spread well-beyond Nvidia with S&P 500 futures now up 3.9%, gold up 3.6% and 2-year yields up 10 basis points. 

In terms of statements, the Nvidia board said:

The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

I wonder how high those 'senior levels' of government were. My guess is that it was the very top.

Update: Those suspicions are looking pretty sound as Semafor reports that President Trump joined an Nvidia board meeting by phone to advocate for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO, citing a source familiar with the matter.

In an interview on CNBC, Trump said Juang "did nothing wrong".

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Market outlook for the week of 23rd - 27th November
item.description:
Monday will start with manufacturing PMI and services PMI from the eurozone, the U.K. and the U.S. while Tuesday we'll get the U.S. CB consumer confidence and the Richmond manufacturing index.

Wednesday the highlight will be the inflation data for Australia. For Japan we'll get the BoJ core CPI y/y and then the focus will shift to the U.S. where we will get the core PCE price index m/m, the prelim GDP q/q, the unemployment claims and the durable goods orders m/m. 

Thursday will be a quiet day in terms of scheduled economic events with the U.S. celebrating Thanksgiving Day. Finally, on Friday the only notable event will be the Tokyo core CPI y/y. 

The consensus for the Australian CPI m/m is 0.4% vs. 0.8% prior. The trimmed mean CPI m/m is expected at 0.3% vs. 0.3% previously and the CPI y/y is expected to rise from 4.3% to 4.8%.

Australian inflation is likely to see a notable rise, especially in the y/y data with Westpac analysts noting that this will be the fastest pace in the series' short history. The main reasons for this spike are the higher fuel prices and the fading impact of last year’s household subsidies.

The focus will be on services inflation, which provides a clearer indication of domestic price pressures. Recent business surveys have offered mixed signals, with services PMIs pointing to continued cost increases, while the NAB survey suggests businesses have limited room to pass higher costs on to consumers.

This week's release will be important to watch because stronger than expected inflation figures, especially in services, could increase market expectations for additional RBA rate hikes, supporting the Australian dollar. Meanwhile, a softer reading could reinforce expectations of rates remaining on hold. 

The Bank noted that the recent strength observed in inflation suggests domestic production capacity is under higher pressure than it previously assessed. That said, monetary policy decisions work with a lag and the impact of the latest five rate hikes are still working its way through the economy, analysts from Wells Fargo said.

In the U.S., the consensus for the core PCE price index m/m is 0.3% compared to 0.3% previously. Personal income m/m is expected to rise by 0.4% vs. 0.2% prior, while personal spending m/m is forecast at 0.4% vs. the prior 0.5%.

The latest retail sales data points to continued strength in household demand, supported by a 0.6% increase in control-group sales and another monthly rise in food-services spending. This resilience could also lead to an upward revision to Q3 GDP, with real consumer spending growth potentially reaching 4.2% annualized.

This suggests that consumer spending is likely to remain solid in October, with both personal income and spending expected to increase. However, the strong pace of consumption seen over the middle of the year is unlikely to continue, according to Wells Fargo.

The boost from larger tax refunds has faded, wage growth has eased somewhat, and weaker equity markets could limit the positive wealth effect on household spending. Consumer demand is still expected to support economic growth into year-end, but at a more moderate pace. Further ahead, easing inflation could help strengthen real disposable income and provide more sustainable support for spending early next year.

U.S. consumer spending remains important for the monetary policy outlook, as persistent household demand could make inflation more difficult to bring down, reinforcing expectations of further Fed tightening beyond December and potentially providing additional support to the U.S. dollar. Conversely, weaker spending could reduce expectations of further rate hikes.

According to the CME FedWatch Tool, at the time of writing markets are pricing in a 25 bps Fed rate hike in December, with futures indicating a probability of roughly 95%.

In Japan the consensus for the Tokyo core CPI y/y is 2.9% vs. 2.6% prior. This week's print will be particularly important for traders, as it will be the last one ahead of the BoJ's December meeting.

If inflation prints in line with expectations it will indicate that price pressures remain firm, strengthening the case for further monetary tightening by the BoJ. According to a Reuters survey, 61 of 71 economists forecast a 25 bps rate hike.

Governor Ueda has signalled that further rate hikes remain likely, noting that monetary conditions are still accommodative and that the yen's weakness could lead to inflation shooting above target.

This article was written by Gina Constantin at investinglive.com.

Key Findings:

  • UK private sector output growth slows in November, despite fastest upturn in manufacturing output for over two years

Comment:

Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence said

“November sees sustained business growth, according to the preliminary flash PMI surveys, pointing to a robust 0.6% increase in GDP during the fourth quarter. Encouragingly, business confidence has improved, with optimism about the year ahead regaining the levels seen prior to the outbreak of war in the Middle East back in February, indicating that the recent Budget has been generally well received by the business community. However, an exception is employment, which showed a renewed fall as companies continue to worry over rising costs and seek to boost productivity. The impact of high energy prices was again exacerbated by high staffing costs, the latter partly blamed by business on government policy."
“The combination of resilient output growth and stubbornly elevated inflation meanwhile makes another rate hike by the Bank of England at its December meeting a near certainty, and raises the likelihood of another hike in February. However, policymakers will likely remain data dependent, as not only did the PMI price gauges signal some cooling of inflationary pressure, but service sector growth also weakened, in part due to the impact of rising interest rates, leaving manufacturing, which is enjoying an AI-related investment led growth spurt, as the main driver of the economic upturn."

UK private sector activity continued to expand in November, although growth slowed slightly. The slowdown was driven by weaker services activity, while manufacturing output accelerated to its strongest pace since August 2024, supported by demand linked to AI data centre investment and higher defence spending. New business increased only modestly, with services firms facing particularly weak export demand. Employment also declined again, mainly due to job cuts in the services sector amid elevated payroll costs and efforts to improve productivity.

On the inflation front, input cost inflation eased to a three-month low, although pressures remained historically elevated due to higher energy, transportation, raw material and wage costs. Output price inflation also slowed to its weakest pace since July. Looking ahead, business confidence improved for a second consecutive month, reaching its highest level since February, with both manufacturers and service providers becoming more optimistic. Overall, the UK economy remains in expansion, but weaker services activity, declining employment and persistent cost pressures remain key concerns.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

  • Prior 52.7

  • Prior 51.7

Key findings:

  • Eurozone growth sustained despite deepening downturn in France

Comment:

Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence said

“At the headline level, the flash PMI data signal sustained steady growth for the eurozone in November, consistent with the economy growing at a near 0.3% pace in the fourth quarter. But this overall picture of continuing economic resilience masks worrying divergences in performance within the euro area. While growth in Germany has accelerated to the fastest for four and a half years, as its manufacturing sector enjoys a growth spurt of the likes not seen for over five years, France is suffering a deepening downturn."
“Just as manufacturers of business equipment and machinery are enjoying their day in the sun amid surging investment spending on defence and AI-related technologies, boosting Germany’s economy in particular, uncertainty about the pollical environment, social unrest and the high cost of living are hitting service providers especially hard, especially for consumer-facing businesses, dampening growth both in France and across the rest of the region as a whole."
“Higher interest rates are also starting to show up as an increasing drag, and the elevated price signals from the PMI alongside the broad message of steady economic growth across the eurozone will support calls for a further rate hike from the ECB in December. However, lower oil prices have helped tame inflationary pressures somewhat in November, leading to slower growth of costs in both manufacturing and services, while slumping demand is reducing sellers’ pricing power in many cases, most notably in France’s service sector, where prices barely rose. Alongside the soft looking labour market indicators from the survey, the slower price growth could ease some concerns about the persistence of elevated inflation if it persists, but for now the surveys send a clear hawkish signal of inflation still running well ahead of the ECB’s 2% target in the coming months.”

The expansion was driven by stronger manufacturing activity, particularly in Germany, where output grew at its fastest pace since March 2022. This offset a deepening downturn in France, where business activity contracted at its fastest pace in six months. New orders increased for a fifth consecutive month, while manufacturing purchasing activity reached a four and a half year high. Employment remained broadly unchanged, as stronger manufacturing hiring was offset by continued job cuts in services.

Looking ahead, business confidence deteriorated for a fourth consecutive month, falling to its lowest level since May, with France recording particularly pessimistic expectations. On the inflation front, input cost pressures remained elevated but eased to a three-month low, while output price inflation slowed to its weakest pace since August. Supply chain pressures also intensified, with supplier delivery times lengthening to their greatest extent since June. Overall, the eurozone economy remains in modest expansion, but the growing divergence between Germany and France and weakening business confidence point to an uneven momentum.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Key findings:

  • German Composite PMI climbs to highest since March 2022

Comment:

Phil Smith, Economics Associate Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence said

"The slowdown in growth at the start of the fourth quarter proved short-lived, with November's provisional PMI results showing the Composite Output Index resume its recent ascent and move to its highest since March 2022. "Encouragingly, alongside the sustained upturn in manufacturing, which continues to see support from rising export orders, demand also revived in the more domestic-oriented service sector and showed the strongest improvement in more than a year, hinting at a broadening recovery. "Labour market conditions remain subdued, although it's notable that manufacturing employment has returned to growth amid increasing pressure on factory capacity and an improvement in business expectations, ending the longest sequence of manufacturing job cuts in the survey's history and perhaps signalling growing confidence among goods producers in the durability of the recovery."

Manufacturing remained the main growth driver, with output expanding at its fastest pace in over five years, while services activity also reached a one-year high. Underlying demand improved significantly, with new orders rising at the fastest pace in more than four and a half years, supported by stronger domestic demand and export sales. Manufacturing employment returned to growth for the first time in nearly three and a half years, although overall employment declined slightly due to continued job cuts in services.

Business confidence improved to a nine-month high, driven by stronger optimism among manufacturers, whose expectations reached their highest level since February. Services firms, however, became less optimistic and continued to reduce staffing levels. On the inflation front, input cost pressures remained historically elevated but eased to a three-month low, while output price inflation accelerated slightly, mainly reflecting more aggressive price increases in the services sector.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
